messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Eleanor Hayes had been reviewing a chain-of-custody log in her county forensic laboratory when the assailant broke through the glass partition. The struggle was sudden and physical, a tangle of limbs and pressure that left distinct marks on her right forearm and left collarbone. In the weeks that followed, Eleanor found herself unable to move through the lab without scanning those specific body parts for reassurance. She always sat with her back against the wall to see the room, a posture that formed steadily and settled into her daily rhythm, allowing her to watch the aisles and the door simultaneously. She avoided exercise, stepping away from the physical exertion that once felt routine, and she avoided eating or restricted her food as a way of coping, often drawing her plates away and leaving portions largely untouched. These habits occupied her days as she continued her forensic work, neither preceding nor resulting from one another, simply sharing the same space. Her mind did not settle the assault away quickly. When the memories surfaced, Eleanor experienced them as a surge of intense rage that rose through her chest, sharp and immediate. Yet, just as the fury arrived, she found herself pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, halting the recollection in mid-stretch. On other days, she recalled what had happened with clarity but felt completely numb, as if the struggle had belonged to a stranger. The laboratory environment amplified certain moments. When a colleague asked about her plans for the coming year, Eleanor felt a familiar tension; talking about the future felt suddenly weighty. If anyone mentioned her bruised forearm or the mark on her collarbone, her eyes locked onto the specific body parts, the visual cues acting as quiet anchors. Simply hearing her own voice describe what had happened to her triggered the same familiar pull, drawing her back into the immediate aftermath. Eleanor’s understanding of herself and her capacity shifted, though these changes unfolded alongside her existing symptoms rather than driving them. She had come to believe that she was inadequate, that her response to the physical confrontation had fallen short of what was expected. She also harbored a firm conviction that if she thought about the event, she would not be able to handle it. This thought avoidance shaped her approach to her case files and team briefings. She used to be a happy person, but now she was always miserable, a quiet shift that she noted without surprise. Her marriage remained steady, her husband present at their home, but Eleanor’s internal landscape had altered. Her appraisals, her memory qualities, and her maladaptive strategies sat together in her life, each distinct yet equally present. The accumulation of these quiet shifts eventually led her to schedule her first appointment. It was not a single breaking point but a convergence of habits and interpretations that had grown heavy over the months. She found herself restricting her food more often, her back finding the wall at every opportunity, and her mind cycling between sudden rage and detached numbness. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in the lab when a routine discussion about upcoming case deadlines made her realize she was bracing for a future she did not recognize. She stepped into the clinic hoping to understand her reactions, though she did not yet know what would change. Most of all, she feared the possibility that thinking about the event might overwhelm her, while quietly hoping that she might, eventually, stop moving through her days as though perpetually braced for another collision.
